episode_thesis: SMN's founders argue trend following needs no forecast, only a broad portfolio that will contain large outliers, so they keep equal long and short risk (to keep crisis alpha), avoid overfitting, and widen the universe to over 200 markets, including synthetic and illiquid alternative markets that correlate little with classic futures. They manage risk with an average volatility target plus per-position budgets, execute illiquid markets with algorithms, and see no arbitrage of outliers after the zero-rate lost decade.

speakers.name: Michael Nobow
speakers.role: Co-founder of SMN (the N in SMN), Vienna systematic CTA since 1997; ex-Austrian bank derivatives trader
speakers.speaker_note: Caption spelling 'Michael nobow'; three-speaker conversation (host plus two guests), speakers separable by who answers. Statements about performance are firm self-reports.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following needs no forecast; the single assumption is that a broadly diversified portfolio will contain large trend outliers over time.
worldview_premises.support: Core philosophy after 27 years; no formal proof.

worldview_premises.premise: The location of the next outlier cannot be predicted from history (cocoa, historically negative-return, was the best CTA market in 2024), so tilting signals to what worked is overfitting.
Short signals in equities and bonds are needed for crisis alpha; removing them would improve a backtest over 30 years of bull markets but destroy crisis protection.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning about backtest vs crisis alpha.

worldview_premises.premise: More markets means more chances to catch outliers; market diversification is in SMN's DNA.
worldview_premises.support: Started with about 70 markets in 1996 and kept widening.

worldview_premises.premise: Synthetic markets (baskets or spreads) create return streams that differ from the underlying and add diversification.
worldview_premises.support: Idea that a combination curve differs from its two inputs.

worldview_premises.premise: Alternative (illiquid, regional) markets move on local factors, not on the global risk-on/risk-off regime, so correlate little with a classic futures portfolio.
Alpha in small markets is capacity-limited: multi-billion funds cannot use them, so only a mid-sized CTA can make them a real return source.
Allocators prefer the biggest CTA shops because of career risk, and flow chases performance: after drawdowns they say trend following does not work, after good years they add.
worldview_premises.support: Observed for 30 years; 2008 crisis redemptions despite crisis alpha.

worldview_premises.premise: Medium and long-term trend following is the most robust horizon; short-term systems were dropped around 2007-08.

Trend following cannot be arbitraged away because outliers have causes beyond CTA trading, though more noise may create more false signals; the 2009-2020 lost decade was artificial (zero rates, QE) and long quiet periods are followed by bigger moves.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from policy regime; 'as we see now'.

worldview_premises.premise: A style shift in a live track record should never be done, so new ideas such as discretionary overlays are tested only in a side fund; the discretionary-plus-systematic mix failed.

speakers.name: Joseph Valin
speakers.role: Head of quantitative research and risk management at SMN (joined 2006)
speakers.speaker_note: Caption 'Joseph valin'; background in business administration and discretionary trading with quantitative support.

worldview_premises.premise: Dispersion among trend-following CTAs is explained more by market universe and position-sizing logic than by signal design, though biased signals (long bias in bonds and equities) add dispersion.
worldview_premises.support: Discussed on a prep call; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Over-optimisation of the past is the main research risk; backtests are judged by a standard set of rules for realism.
Alternative markets are cycle-driven by local supply and demand, with medium to long-term cycles trend systems capture well, at different times from classic markets.
Volatility is a non-directional asset class that needs its own signal design rather than the plain price-momentum rule.
worldview_premises.support: VIX behaviour in the lost decade.

worldview_premises.premise: Slippage in illiquid markets is hard to know ex ante, so high assumptions are used.
worldview_premises.support: Smallest markets about four to five times classic slippage.

steps.to: Use deliberately high slippage plus broker execution costs
Sharpe of whole portfolio still rises significantly

steps.to: Enhanced model with price momentum, vol of vol and curve shape
Hourly curve snapshots with quick intraday exits

decision_process.practice: Volatility target is an annualised standard deviation goal met on average over the long run; no re-levering on days with few signals.
decision_process.why: Positions come only from long/medium-term trend signals.

decision_process.practice: Each position has a risk budget/stop limit to control drawdown, complementing the symmetric standard deviation target.
After a huge price move in one market (cocoa) with the exit far below price, positions are cut; limits are broad so ordinary moves do not trigger cuts.
Trade illiquid markets with execution algos (TWAP-style) over a day or two with per-market instructions.
decision_process.why: Positions need more than one session.

decision_process.practice: Synthetics: risk-parity baskets (S&P vs 10-year note, 2009) and correlation spreads between related commodities (NY vs London cocoa, wheat types, South African maize and soybeans); host cites 20-25% of risk.
Standard rules for evaluating whether a backtest is realistic.
VIX via enhanced momentum (price momentum, vol of vol, curve shape), hourly monitoring.

speakers.evidence_style: Backtests with stress costs and realism rules; practical execution detail.

current_views.view: Dispersion in trend following in 2023-24 is mainly universe and sizing, with some signal bias effect.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Correction applied: the 20-25% synthetic risk share was read by the host from a Hedge Fund Journal article; SMN did not confirm it.
The claim that adding illiquid markets raises Sharpe 'significantly' after costs is stated with no figures; slippage multiple is from memory ('I don't have the number').
Michael's explanation of why synthetic markets add diversification rests on the idea that a combination curve looks different from its inputs, with no test shown.
2008 crisis alpha did not attract assets; the argument that small size is the only differentiator assumes allocator behaviour not shown.
Statement that the lost decade was 'artificial' and that quiet periods precede big moves is asserted without evidence.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs: none are used as forecasts; SMN says it is agnostic to direction. Observable input for the thesis is the presence of large outliers after long quiet periods and policy regimes (zero rates, QE) that suppress them (years); correlation of alternative markets vs classic (ongoing); allocator flows follow performance (annual).
reader_inferences: (reader) SMN's edge claim rests on capacity: the alternative-markets Sharpe uplift likely shrinks if the firm grows.
(reader) 'No forecast, symmetrical signals' is a robustness choice that pays in crisis at the cost of some backtest return.
(reader) The 20-25% synthetic share quoted by the host is unconfirmed, so risk allocation to synthetics is uncertain.
